Euclidean geometry. The mathematical system of plane and solid geometry founded on Euclid's five axioms and the parallel postulate, codified in The Elements around three hundred BCE. It describes the geometry of flat space where familiar rules hold. Parallel lines never meet. Angles in a triangle sum to one hundred eighty degrees. The Pythagorean theorem governs right triangles. For two millennia, Euclidean geometry was synonymous with geometry itself until the nineteenth century discovery of non-Euclidean alternatives shattered this monopoly.

The five axioms of Euclidean geometry state that segments can be drawn between any two points, a line can be extended indefinitely, a circle can be drawn from any center and radius, all right angles are equal, and the parallel postulate. The parallel postulate is the most controversial of these. It states that through a point not on a line, exactly one parallel line exists. This single assumption distinguishes Euclidean from non-Euclidean geometries and sparked centuries of mathematical debate.

The Elements consisted of thirteen books containing approximately four hundred sixty-five propositions. It was the dominant geometry textbook for over two thousand years, establishing the axiomatic method as the standard for mathematical proof and rigor in Western civilization. Euclid proved foundational theorems: the Pythagorean theorem, the fact that angles in triangles always sum to one hundred eighty degrees in Euclidean space, properties of circles and inscribed polygons, and constructions using only compass and straightedge. The axiomatic method, starting from simple axioms and deriving theorems via logical deduction, became the gold standard for mathematical rigor and influenced philosophy and science for millennia.

In the nineteenth century, Gauss, Lobachevsky, and Bolyai independently discovered hyperbolic geometry, where the parallel postulate fails and through a point, infinitely many parallels exist. Riemann developed elliptic geometry, also called spherical geometry, where no parallels exist and the angle sum in triangles exceeds one hundred eighty degrees. This showed that non-Euclidean geometries are logically consistent alternatives. The discovery of non-Euclidean geometries revealed that Euclid's axioms describe only one possible space. Einstein's relativity theory later demonstrated that the universe's actual geometry is non-Euclidean at cosmic scales. Yet Euclidean geometry remains the most intuitive and practical for everyday phenomena, engineering, and classical physics, even though it is not the geometry of the universe on large scales.
